View of Delft. Vermeer's painting, created circa 1660 to 1661, is his only known cityscape—a serene panorama of Delft's skyline reflected in the Schie River after rain. Its atmospheric handling of light, sky, and urban architecture has made it a cornerstone of landscape painting and a meditation on the transience of weather and human settlement.

The painting depicts the real southern face of Delft, with the Schiedam Gate and tower of the New Church rising above a foreground of boats and figures on the waterfront. Painted from across the river, the low vantage point and calm water create an almost mirror-like reflection that emphasises the composition's geometric stability. The work captures the moment after a rainstorm; sunlight breaks through clouds, illuminating the city's red-tiled roofs and pale facades with extraordinary subtlety.

The painting measures approximately 98 by 117 centimetres and is housed in the Mauritshuis museum in The Hague. The work invites comparison to seventeenth-century Dutch landscape painting traditions, yet Vermeer's restraint and atmospheric precision set it apart as uniquely his own. Long considered a supreme achievement of landscape art, it influenced the Impressionists in the nineteenth century. This masterwork of landscape and light remains his only documented cityscape and exemplifies the Dutch Golden Age fascination with mapping and depicting the Dutch landscape, sharing with his other works the interplay of light and domestic Dutch life.
